tiles.title: Avoiding unintended mutations through shared references / Counting values with collections.Counter

steps.title: Avoiding unintended mutations through shared references

blocks.text: Different names can refer to one object: assignment is not a copy. Mutating a shared list or dictionary can be visible through another name and to a caller.
items.copy() or items[:] makes a shallow list copy: top-level changes are independent, but references to existing elements remain. A nested mutable element can still be shared.

blocks.title: Separate outer lists, shared inner list
blocks.alt_text: original and alias point to one outer list. copied points to another outer list. Both outer lists reference the same existing inner list. An append through alias changes the shared outer list; a nested update through copied changes the shared inner list.

blocks.text: alias and original share an outer list, so appending through alias affects original. copied has a separate outer list, so that append does not affect its top level. Updating an existing inner element through copied is visible through original because the inner list is shared. original[:] also makes a shallow copy.

blocks.code:
original = [[3, 2]]
alias = original
copied = original.copy()
alias.append([5])
copied[0][0] = 9
print(original)
print(copied)

blocks.text: After from collections import Counter, Counter(items) counts occurrences of hashable elements, mapping each element to its count. Use it to summarize repeated stationery labels.
counts.most_common(1) returns a list containing the most frequent element/count pair, or an empty list for an empty counter. Check that the list is nonempty before selecting its first pair.
most_common orders pairs by descending count. Tied counts follow first encounter, not a separate ranking. Compare the repeated-label example with empty input and a tie using the same labels.

from collections import Counter

print(counts)

print(pairs)

    print(label, count)

steps.title: Inspecting program state with diagnostic printing

blocks.text: Use print(label, value) for a labeled view of the state at an execution point. Observe the text before conversion and the quantity after its binding rather than guessing from a final result.
repr(value) returns a printable representation that can expose details ordinary string display obscures. Here it makes surrounding spaces and quotes visible.

Place the diagnostic after the binding or before the operation you are investigating. A print before a later reassignment cannot show the later value. Remove the print call when that diagnostic output is no longer needed.

blocks.code:
def convert_quantity(text):
    text = ' 3 '
    print("raw text", repr(text))
    quantity = int(text)
    print("converted quantity", quantity)
    return quantity

convert_quantity(' 3 ')

Observe after the quantity binding. Output: converted quantity 3

blocks.text: Document public functions, modules, classes and methods with docstrings so callers can inspect the interface.

A string literal first in a function body provides its docstring. Start with a concise purpose summary; separate additional calling details with a blank line. A string later in the body is not its first-statement docstring.

Describe arguments, return values and applicable exceptions accurately. For cost, document the numeric arguments and returned product without inventing exception claims. help(cost) displays the function signature and documentation, including its docstring.

def cost(quantity, unit_price):
    """Calculate an order cost.
